nameStory: The planehead filefish gets its name from its distinctively flattened, plane-like head profile when viewed from the side. The 'filefish' part comes from their rough, sandpaper-like skin that feels like a metal file when rubbed the wrong way - early fishermen actually used dried filefish skin as sandpaper for woodworking!
description: The planehead filefish is a peculiar-looking marine fish with a compressed, oval body and a notably flat head profile. These small fish typically grow to about 4-6 inches long and have a single prominent spine on their back instead of a traditional first dorsal fin. Their skin feels remarkably rough and sandpaper-like to the touch, covered in tiny, bristle-like scales that give them excellent camouflage among seaweeds and coral.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Laterally compressed, oval body with a distinctively flattened head profile that looks like it was pressed flat - the head appears almost triangular when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Single prominent dorsal spine instead of a first dorsal fin, followed by a soft-rayed dorsal fin; tail fin is rounded and fan-shaped

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Mottled brown, gray, and olive coloration with irregular patches and spots that help them blend with seaweed; can change color slightly to match surroundings

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, terminal mouth at the front tip of the snout with protruding teeth visible even when mouth is closed; designed for picking at small prey

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small fish reaching 4-6 inches in length, with a deep body that's about half as tall as it is long

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Skin feels extremely rough like coarse sandpaper when rubbed backward, covered in tiny bristle-like scales called shagreen

habitat: Planehead filefish inhabit coastal waters along New England's rocky shores and areas with abundant seaweed beds, typically in depths of 10-60 feet. They prefer areas with good cover like eelgrass beds, kelp forests, and rocky reefs where they can hide among the vegetation. These fish are most commonly found in warmer months when water temperatures rise, often around jetties, piers, and shallow coastal areas with structure.

seasonality.spring: Begin appearing in New England waters as temperatures warm, usually found in deeper areas initially before moving to shallower coastal zones.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for observation when they're most active in shallow eelgrass beds and around rocky structures, often seen picking at algae and small invertebrates.
seasonality.fall: Still present but may start moving to slightly deeper waters as temperatures cool, continuing to feed actively before winter.
seasonality.winter: Rare to absent from New England waters, having moved south to warmer coastal areas or deeper offshore waters.

funFact: Filefish can actually lock themselves into crevices by erecting their dorsal spine and pressing their rough belly against rocks - they become so wedged in that they're nearly impossible to pull out, making them masters of hide-and-seek in the underwater world!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small marine fish with compressed bodies, but the combination of the single prominent dorsal spine, extremely rough skin, and flattened head profile is unique. Remember: if it feels like sandpaper and has that distinctive 'ironed flat' head, it's a filefish!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'filefish,' they're not closely related to other fish with 'file' in their name. They belong to the same order as pufferfish and triggerfish, sharing the characteristic of having a modified first dorsal fin (in this case, reduced to a single spine). The rough skin that gives them their name was historically valuable to fishermen as a natural abrasive.
compareHints: Since planehead filefish is the only Stephanolepis species commonly found in New England waters, compare it to other filefish in the family Monacanthidae by looking for the distinctively flattened head profile. Other filefish in the region tend to have more rounded or pointed head profiles, while the planehead's compressed, plane-like head shape is quite distinctive among its relatives.
